title: NAO 2025–26: budgets, rail audits, devolution and who follows up public inquiries
label: 20 October 2026 · NAO annual report evidence
summary: The National Audit Office's leadership explained why the NAO came in under budget for 2025–26, what they learned from auditing rail companies taken into public ownership, how the new Local Audit Office will affect local audit and devolution, staffing and technology plans, performance on timely accounts and value-for-money work, and whether the NAO should follow up implementation of public inquiry recommendations. The NAO welcomed the Local Audit Office but warned capacity will take years to build, defended prudence over a supplementary estimate, described improvements in audit timeliness, and urged careful design before taking on follow-up of inquiry recommendations to avoid mission creep.

Assessing whether public money is used effectively to achieve intended outcomes.

chapters.title: Budget outcome and the supplementary estimate
chapters.takeaway: The NAO underspent by about £2m because specialist audit costs were lower than expected and fee income was higher; asking for a supplementary estimate earlier was prudent.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You came in under budget by roughly £2 million split between lower spending and higher income—what drove each?

turns.speaker: Gareth Davies
turns.text: On expenditure, staff costs were about on plan but we spent less on specialist advice than we budgeted for—mainly on the new audits of train operating companies. On income, we got more fee-funded work than expected, better building rental and the timing of audit work meant more income recognised at year end.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You requested a £1.2m supplementary estimate but still came in under—why not manage it internally?

turns.speaker: Gareth Davies
turns.text: When we asked for the money we did not know income would cover extra costs. It would have been reckless to assume that. The NAO must avoid overspending that would cause an excess vote; prudence was the right call.

turns.speaker: Rebecca Sheeran
turns.text: We're at mid-year now and have done a detailed review: this year’s projections are tight but within budget. We have clarity about the workload this year, so we don't expect another supplementary estimate.

chapters.title: Auditing rail companies and capacity planning
chapters.takeaway: Auditing train operating companies taught the NAO a lot, the first wave was completed on time, and the experience informs budgeting for further transfers into public ownership.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What impact did auditing the nationalised rail companies have on your resources—and what does it teach you about future additional burdens?

turns.speaker: Gareth Davies
turns.text: We audited seven operating companies in 2025–26. Teams planned carefully and drew on previous auditors' work, so no surprises and all seven signed off before the summer recess. We have three more coming in and will use the lessons to budget and plan.

turns.speaker: Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown
turns.text: Does the Local Audit Office free up your resources as local audit work shifts away from the NAO?

turns.speaker: Gareth Davies
turns.text: I welcome the Local Audit Office. It won’t simply free up NAO resources—our work will shift in focus toward assessing how devolution delivers value for money, and we’ll need to collaborate closely with the LAO.

turns.speaker: Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown
turns.text: Will local auditors have enough capacity to take on more work quickly?

turns.speaker: Gareth Davies
turns.text: Capacity will take years to build. Bill Butler’s early appointment is helpful, but there will be an interim period where the NAO may need to do more until local capability matures.

turns.speaker: Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown
turns.text: Do you have powers to investigate mayoral authorities when things go wrong?

turns.speaker: Gareth Davies
turns.text: We have limited powers created after the Audit Commission's abolition, but they exclude scrutinising individual authorities. For comparative work across devolved systems we need clearer access powers to strategic authorities; we’ve asked government for that.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Where will the Local Audit Office sit for accountability—will Parliament have a route to question it?

turns.speaker: Gareth Davies
turns.text: The LAO will be an arm’s-length ministerial body in MHCLG, accountable to the Secretary of State. Parliament can still call its senior people—Bill Butler is due as a witness—and PAC will engage with its work.

chapters.title: Performance measures, staff and technology
chapters.takeaway: The NAO has grown staff numbers but expects headcount to level; AI and new tools are improving productivity; audit timeliness has improved but targets remain ambitious.

turns.speaker: John Glen
turns.text: Staff numbers have risen by nearly 25% in five years—why, and will this level off?

turns.speaker: Gareth Davies
turns.text: Growth reflects more and more complex audits, higher audit standards and investment in capability. Our April estimate for the current year was essentially flat and growth has levelled off; productivity gains from audit technology and AI will help going forward.

turns.speaker: John Glen
turns.text: If you could bring forward more investment in years one and two, would you do so—are accounting profiles limiting optimal investment?

turns.speaker: Gareth Davies
turns.text: Money helps, but organisational capacity to absorb change matters too. We’ve rolled out Copilot and other tools, and we’re planning a three-year programme to modernise audits rather than one big spend that the organisation couldn't absorb quickly.

turns.speaker: Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown
turns.text: Could AI just mean shedding lower-level staff?

turns.speaker: Gareth Davies
turns.text: Not so far. The big firms still recruit graduates and school leavers but train them differently with a stronger digital emphasis. Junior roles are changing rather than disappearing.

turns.speaker: Chris Vince
turns.text: You missed your 70% pre-recess certification target in the year covered—what happened?

turns.speaker: Gareth Davies
turns.text: In 2025 we missed that target, but we learned from it and reached 70% by the 2026 summer recess. We expect more than 90% finished by the end of October and are targeting 100% by the end of October next year.

turns.speaker: Chris Vince
turns.text: Value for money (VFM) reports score well internally but MPs rate them lower—why?

turns.speaker: Gareth Davies
turns.text: Different audiences judge quality differently. MPs' views matter and we’re improving outreach—newsletters, researcher engagement—and asking how to make our VFM work more accessible and useful to them.

turns.speaker: Rebecca Sheeran
turns.text: On staff exits, we ran a voluntary exit scheme to rebalance skills for the new strategy; the payback on those exits is under a year and helped manage our cost base.

turns.speaker: John Glen
turns.text: Turnover is below target—does that risk stagnation?

turns.speaker: Gareth Davies
turns.text: Low turnover is a better problem than high turnover. We use performance management, learning and selective voluntary exits to keep energy and progression opportunities in the organisation.

chapters.title: Risks, inquiry follow-up and the chair’s reflections
chapters.takeaway: The NAO narrowed principal risks for executive focus, has improved wellbeing metrics, and is open to examining whether it should check implementation of public inquiry recommendations—if government fixes monitoring arrangements and independence is preserved.

turns.speaker: Sarah Olney
turns.text: You reduced principal risks from 24 to nine—does that mean less detailed risk management?

turns.speaker: Rebecca Sheeran
turns.text: No. We aligned risks to strategy at board level while keeping a bottom-up set of component risks and business-owner assessments to retain detail.

turns.speaker: Sarah Olney
turns.text: You flagged poor service delivery and failure to deliver impact as concerns—why?

turns.speaker: Rebecca Sheeran
turns.text: We raised the ambition of our strategy, so the risk is we don't fully deliver the bigger impact we’ve set ourselves. We’re strengthening parliamentary engagement and communications to mitigate that.

turns.speaker: Sarah Olney
turns.text: Sickness and wellbeing were principal risks last year but not this year—what changed?

turns.speaker: Rebecca Sheeran
turns.text: They’re now component risks feeding into a principal risk about culture. Sickness absence has fallen to about 5.2 days per FTE and we’ve invested in wellbeing and performance management.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: On inquiry follow-up: should the NAO hold government to account for implementing public inquiry recommendations?

turns.speaker: Gareth Davies
turns.text: We've been asked to consider that. The NAO could audit whether the government has implemented agreed actions, but first there must be a reliable government system for tracking recommendations. We must avoid becoming part of the system we should audit—careful design is essential to prevent mission creep.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Some feel an independent body should ensure inquiry recommendations are implemented—do you see a role for that?

turns.speaker: Gareth Davies
turns.text: There's a legitimate case, but it’s for Parliament and government to decide the governance. We can contribute practical experience, but we’d need clear boundaries and an evidence base from inspectorates where specialist judgments are required.

turns.speaker: Dame Fiona Reynolds
turns.text: We’d be cautious and set strict terms if involved. It would be a third-line check on implementation rather than judging clinical or specialist practice directly.

turns.speaker: Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown
turns.text: PAC heard calls for an independent standing body to handle schemes and recommendations—might NAO audit those schemes?

turns.speaker: Gareth Davies
turns.text: We already audit compensation schemes financially. The question here is whether we should audit the implementation of inquiry recommendations more broadly; it requires a government framework to make that audit meaningful.

turns.speaker: Dame Fiona Reynolds
turns.text: On a personal note as I finish my term: NAO quality and strategic focus have strengthened. Challenges ahead include AI, devolution, and longer-term issues like climate and social care where stability would help.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you—this was your last annual report session as chair. We appreciate your service.

turns.speaker: Dame Fiona Reynolds
turns.text: Thank you. It's been a privilege. The NAO has become more purposeful and focused on impact, and I’m proud of the progress.
